extracted.intended_audience: U.S. policymakers, diplomats, and French ministers (readers of Jefferson's correspondence)
extracted.subtask_description: Private/public letters by a diplomat (Thomas Jefferson) analysing commercial policy, the whale-fishery, and recommended state trade measures between the United States and France (late 18th century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce regulation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of the United States is, to use neither prohibitions nor premiums. Where a government finds itself under the necessity of undertaking that regulation, it should conduct it as an intelligent merchant would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If government must regulate commerce, it should 'invite customers to purchase, by facilitating their means of payment, and by adapting goods to their taste.' Jefferson specifies two operations for government with respect to U.S. commerce in France: (1) to do away, or moderate, prohibitions and monopolies on materials for payment; (2) to encourage principal manufactures that new customers call for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate means of payment & adapt goods to market
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite customers to purchase by facilitating their means of payment, and by adapting goods to their taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: encourage simple manufactures (oznaburgs, plains, duffel blankets) used by laboring poor in America so they can be received in French ports as acceptable payment for tobacco, rice, and whale-oil; proposed instrument: a 5% export premium for ten years (only paid if exports materialize). Jefferson provides calculations of quantities and values to show the potential employment and exchange benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation law principle (export shipping restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our navigation law (if it be wise to have any) should be the reverse of that of England. Instead of confining importations to home-bottoms, or those of the producing nation, we should confine exportations to home-bottoms, or to those of nations having treaties with us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a policy tool to nourish a maritime force and create employment for seamen; Jefferson cites French arrangements for tobacco and whale-oils being receivable only in French or American bottoms to employ near two thousand seamen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of commercial regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce requires steady regulations; the dignity of legislation admits not of changes backwards and forwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson warns that 'sudden vicissitudes of opening and shutting ports, do little injury to merchants settled on the opposite coast... But they ruin the adventurer, whose distance requires six months’ notice.' Policy should avoid abrupt reversals (e.g., Arrêts that open then close markets), because they destroy long-distance enterprises and undermine markets and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shipping/port rules to favour national seamen and trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict receipt of key imports (tobacco, whale-oils, rice) to French or American bottoms to employ seamen and shift employment from foreign (English) hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson cites the Arrêt of December 1787 (that American whale-oils should not be received but in French or American bottoms) and similar measures for tobacco; such rules can immediately put English vessels out of employment and call French and American ones into service, supporting a maritime labor pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness of bounties/subsidies for fisheries
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties and other governmental encouragements to the whale-fishery are costly and must be justified by strategic benefit; the trade is too poor to support itself without large subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson gives concrete figures (English bounties/costs: government paid 15 pounds a man; English cost of 20 pounds per ton of oil in bounty; French required sacrifice estimates of 1,285,200 livres/year for 3,570 seamen or 4–5 million livres/year to match English scale). He argues governments may willingly spend large sums to secure monopoly advantages, but opponents should weigh these subsidies against alternative uses of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare opportunity cost of supporting seamen vs. domestic laborers
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding subsidies, compare the number of people supported and long-term employment effects: supporting fishermen/seamen is costlier per head than fostering laborers/manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson compares maintaining 3,570 seamen at recurring cost (1,285,200 livres/year) versus giving a 5% export-premium to produce permanent employment for 30,000 laborers (calculation: 7,020,000 livres of consumption equals nine million days' work etc.). He frames subsidies as a choice between supporting seamen and supporting many more manufacturers/laborers for less recurring cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinery viability depends on available raw material (market/policy dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A refinery (example: Rouen works) calculated on free access to American oil may fail if confined to French fishery alone for want of matter to work on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson notes the refinery at Rouen 'will cost them half a million of livres; will be able to refine all the oil which can be used in the kingdom,' but its success was calculated on the Arrêt of Dec 29th admitting American produce. If policy restricts inputs, the enterprise's scale and economics change and may make it unviable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinery outcomes as strategic commercial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful refinery can (1) supplant foreign solid spermaceti by producing equal quality at lower price; (2) substitute refined black whale-oil for spermaceti-oil at lower price; (3) convert Brazil oil to tallow-equivalent; (4) expand demand by adapting oils to new uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson enumerates these four effects to argue that refining technology, combined with open import policy, could transform market structure and greatly extend domestic demand for whale-oil derivatives — but again warns that these benefits require sufficient supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spermaceti oil quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Spermaceti oil: luminous; resists coagulation by cold to the forty-first degree of Fahrenheit; yields no smell at all; used within doors; sells at treble the price of common whale-oil in London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note head-matter yields solid spermaceti used in medicine and candles, sold by the pound at double the price of the oil. The fishery for this oil requires boldness and long voyages (9–12 months) and thus carries operational risks (men absent, liable to capture during war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenland whale-oil quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenland whale-oil: resists coagulation by cold to thirty-six degrees Fahrenheit; has an insupportable smell indoors; is not luminous; sells about sixteen pounds the ton in London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fish is clumsy and timid; voyages last about three to four months; yields the fin in quantity (i.e., whale bone products). It is the fishery mostly frequented by European nations due to shorter voyages and less difficult hunting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brazil (small Brazil) whale-oil quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Brazil whale-oil: chills at fifty-two degrees Fahrenheit; is black and offensive; worth about thirteen pounds the ton in London; in warm summer nights it burns better than Greenland oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally found near Nantucket and later in Brazil; its oil is lower-value but could be curdled into tallow by refining methods, improving its marketability and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retroactive or capricious legal changes; respect legislative dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity of legislation admits not of changes backwards and forwards; sudden changes in laws (opening then closing markets) are unjust to merchants and adventurers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson appeals to amity between nations and legislative dignity as reasons to except the United States from a restrictive Arrêt, and warns that reviving prohibitions after prior admissions causes ruin and loss of trust among traders who rely on earlier measures.
